newsitem.title: USA: Cohen to press for Bosnia police force at meeting.
newsitem.headline: Cohen to press for Bosnia police force at meeting.

text.p: U.S. Defence Secretary William Cohen will urge NATO allies to speed development of an international police force for Bosnia at a meeting in Brussels beginning on Thursday, according to a senior defence official.

The official, briefing reporters ahead of a two-day meeting of alliance defence ministers, said the police force, which could be used to hunt and arrest indicted war criminals in Bosnia, was of major importance to Washington.

Cohen will depart on Wednesday and fly first to Brussels before visiting Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, Bahrain, the United Arab Emirates and Oman to discuss joint security in that oil-rich region. He will return home on June 18.

"It (an outside civilian police force) is a matter of concern to the whole U.S. government and I expect there will be discussion on that ... the United States is pushing that very, very hard," the official, who asked not to be identified, said in response to questions on the NATO meeting.

Cohen and other alliance ministers have insisted that a 31,000-member NATO-led military peacekeeping force now in Bosnia should not be used to arrest indicted war criminals. The official told reporters some progress was being made on forming such a force but more work needed to be done on how it would be set up and what nations would provide members.

The Brussels meeting will focus on the upcoming expansion of the alliance to include some former Communist states in Eastern and Central Europe but the problem of arresting and trying indicted criminals has been a festering wound since the Dayton peace accords brought an uneasy peace to Bosnia.

The Middle East stops will be Cohen's first visit as defence secretary to the Gulf, where the United States maintains a major naval presence based in Bahrain and a fleet of warplanes in Saudi Arabia and Kuwait to keep watch over southern Iraq.

The visit, beginning in Saudi Arabia on Saturday, will give Cohen a chance to discuss joint security and U.S. troop protection measures with King Fahd and other leaders in the region. Possible major U.S. fighter jet sales to Saudi Arabia and the UAE could come up in talks with other officials.

The senior U.S. defence official said the Gulf trip was a get-acquainted visit and he did not expect any final report from Saudi Arabia on two car bombings in the kingdom since late 1995 that have killed 24 U.S. troops stationed there.

In addition to meeting Gulf leaders, Cohen will visit U.S. forces in Saudi Arabia, Kuwait and Bahrain, including some 5,000 Americans who were moved to a remote desert airbase in Saudi Arabia after the second car bombing at Dhahran on June 25 of last year that killed 19 American airmen.

He plans to urge the moderate nations of the Gulf Cooperation Council to remain united in a coalition with Washington to keep close watch over Iraq and Iran, which the United States worries could threaten security in the region.

"I think the focus will be on maintaining the coalition. I don't think that there is any special heightened military threat beyond the fact that there is always a problem with respect to Iraq until it decides to comply fully with the U.N. resolutions," the official said.

Although the issue is not on Cohen's formal agenda, the subject of potential multibillion-dollar sales of Lockheed Martin Corp ( ) F-16 jet fighters could come up on his stops in Saudi Arabia and the UAE.

The Saudis have been talking with Lockheed about the possibility of purchasing up to 100 F-16s and the UAE has been exploring the possible purchase of as many as 80 of the little attack jets. They cost some $25 million each, but associated support and maintenance costs push that cost much higher.
"We have made an offer (to the UAE). They are contemplating that offer," the official told reporters.
